## 1.1 · Concurrency, parallelism and asynchrony

| Term | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Concurrency** | Several tasks are in progress during the same period of time, possibly taking turns on a single CPU core | A web server handling many requests |
| **Parallelism** | Several tasks are executed at the same instant, on different CPU cores | Resizing 1000 images on 8 cores |
| **Asynchrony** | The caller is not blocked while an operation (usually I/O) runs; no extra thread is needed | Waiting for a database query without holding a thread |

## 1.2 · Which tool for which work

| Kind of work | Example | Tool |
|---|---|---|
| I/O-bound | HTTP call, database query, file read | `async` / `await` |
| CPU-bound, must not freeze the UI | Image filter in a desktop app | `await Task.Run(...)` |
| CPU-bound, data-parallel | Process every item of a large array | `Parallel.For`, PLINQ |
| Many I/O operations, a few at a time | Call an API for 1000 ids, 10 at a time | `Parallel.ForEachAsync`, `SemaphoreSlim` |
| Recurring work in a web app | Remove expired games every minute | `BackgroundService` |

## 2.1 · Threads

- A thread is an independent path of execution within a process.
- All threads of a process share its memory (the heap).
- Each thread has its own stack.

## 2.2 · History

- Early computers (von Neumann architecture, 1945) had a single processing unit and executed one instruction stream.
- Operating systems introduced **time slicing**: the CPU is switched between threads many times per second, so several programs appear to run at once on one core.
- Since the mid-2000s, CPU clock speeds have barely grown; more cores are added instead. A single-threaded program uses only one of them.

## 2.3 · How threading helps

- **Responsiveness**: a desktop or mobile app keeps the UI thread free while long work is done on another thread.
- **Throughput**: a web server handles many requests at once. With async I/O, a waiting request does not hold a thread, so a limited thread pool serves more requests.
- **Speed**: a large computation is split into chunks that are executed in parallel on several cores.

On a single core, threads do not make computation faster; they only allow switching between tasks.

## 2.4 · `Thread` in C\#

`Thread` (in `System.Threading`) is created with a delegate, started with `Start()` and waited for with `Join()`.

```{.csharp}
const int Steps = 20;
var completedSteps = 0;

// Long-running work: each step takes 50 ms
var worker = new Thread(() =>
{
    for (var i = 0; i < Steps; i++)
    {
        Thread.Sleep(50);
        Interlocked.Increment(ref completedSteps);
    }
});

// Progress is reported by another thread while the work runs
var reporter = new Thread(() =>
{
    while (Volatile.Read(ref completedSteps) < Steps)
    {
        Console.WriteLine($"Progress: {Volatile.Read(ref completedSteps) * 100 / Steps}%");
        Thread.Sleep(200);
    }
    Console.WriteLine("Progress: 100%");
});

worker.Start();
reporter.Start();

worker.Join();
reporter.Join();
```

## 2.5 · Threads in a .NET application

Every .NET process has several threads, for example:

- **Main thread**: runs `Main` (or the top-level statements).
- **Thread pool threads**: run tasks, timers, `async` continuations and ASP.NET Core requests.
- **Finalizer thread**: runs finalizers (`~ClassName()`) of collected objects.
- **Background garbage collection thread**: collects memory while the application keeps running.
- **UI thread** (WinForms, WPF, MAUI): the only thread allowed to update UI controls.

## 2.6 · Foreground and background threads

- A **foreground** thread keeps the process alive: the process exits only when all foreground threads have finished.
- A **background** thread is stopped abruptly when the last foreground thread ends.
- `new Thread(...)` creates a foreground thread by default; `IsBackground = true` changes that.
- Thread pool threads are background threads.

```{.csharp}
var created = new Thread(() => { });
Console.WriteLine($"New thread is background: {created.IsBackground}");

ThreadPool.QueueUserWorkItem(_ =>
    Console.WriteLine($"Thread pool thread is background: {Thread.CurrentThread.IsBackground}"));

Thread.Sleep(100);
```

## 2.7 · Common `Thread` members

- `Start()`: starts the thread.
- `Join()`: waits for the thread to finish. `Join(TimeSpan)` returns `false` if it did not finish in time.
- `Thread.Sleep()`: pauses the **current thread**. The CPU core is given to other threads, but the sleeping thread itself can do nothing else.
- `IsAlive`: `true` while the thread is running.
- `Name`, `ManagedThreadId`: identify the thread, e.g. in logs.
- `IsBackground`: foreground or background thread.
- `Priority`: a hint to the operating system scheduler; rarely needed.
- `Thread.CurrentThread`: the thread executing the current code.
- `Abort()`: not supported since .NET Core; it throws `PlatformNotSupportedException`. Threads are stopped cooperatively with a `CancellationToken`.

## 2.8 · Naming threads

```{.csharp}
var named = new Thread(() =>
    Console.WriteLine($"Running on '{Thread.CurrentThread.Name}', id {Thread.CurrentThread.ManagedThreadId}"))
{
    Name = "MyWorkerThread"
};

Console.WriteLine($"Main thread id: {Thread.CurrentThread.ManagedThreadId}");
named.Start();
named.Join();
```

## 2.9 · Waiting with `Join`

```{.csharp}
var background = new Thread(() =>
{
    for (var i = 0; i < 5; i++)
    {
        Thread.Sleep(100);
        Console.WriteLine($"Worker thread: {i}");
    }
});

background.Start();

for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++)
{
    Thread.Sleep(100);
    Console.WriteLine($"Main thread: {i}");
}

// Blocks the main thread until the worker finishes
background.Join();
Console.WriteLine("Both finished");
```

## 2.10 · `IsAlive` and `Join` with a timeout

```{.csharp}
var sleeper = new Thread(() => Thread.Sleep(500));
sleeper.Start();
Console.WriteLine($"Is alive after Start: {sleeper.IsAlive}");

var finishedInTime = sleeper.Join(TimeSpan.FromMilliseconds(100));
Console.WriteLine($"Finished within 100 ms: {finishedInTime}");

sleeper.Join();
Console.WriteLine($"Is alive after Join: {sleeper.IsAlive}");
```

## 2.11 · Thread pool

- Creating a thread is expensive: an operating system object, around 1 MB of reserved stack, and start-up time.
- The **thread pool** keeps a set of reusable threads and gives them work items from a queue.
- `Task.Run`, `Parallel`, timers, `async` continuations and ASP.NET Core requests all use the thread pool.
- The pool starts with about as many threads as there are cores and adds more only gradually when all of them are busy.
- A blocked pool thread is wasted. When many are blocked, new work waits in the queue: **thread pool starvation**.

```{.csharp}
ThreadPool.GetMinThreads(out var minWorkers, out _);
ThreadPool.GetMaxThreads(out var maxWorkers, out _);
Console.WriteLine($"Min worker threads: {minWorkers}, max: {maxWorkers}");

ThreadPool.QueueUserWorkItem(_ =>
    Console.WriteLine($"Is thread pool thread: {Thread.CurrentThread.IsThreadPoolThread}"));

Thread.Sleep(100);
```

## 2.12 · Thread blocking

```{.csharp}
var actionQueue = new ConcurrentQueue<Action>();
for (var i = 0; i < 10; i++)
{
    var id = i;
    actionQueue.Enqueue(i % 2 == 0
        ? () => Console.WriteLine($"Action {id}: quick")
        : () =>
        {
            Console.WriteLine($"Action {id}: waiting...");
            Thread.Sleep(500); // e.g. a synchronous database call
        });
}

var blockingStopwatch = Stopwatch.StartNew();

var pool = new Thread[2];
for (var i = 0; i < pool.Length; i++)
{
    pool[i] = new Thread(() =>
    {
        while (actionQueue.TryDequeue(out var action))
        {
            action();
        }
    });
    pool[i].Start();
}

foreach (var thread in pool)
{
    thread.Join();
}

Console.WriteLine($"Took {blockingStopwatch.ElapsedMilliseconds} ms");
```

## 3.1 · Race conditions

- A **race condition** is a bug where the result depends on the timing of threads.
- The most common forms:
  - **lost update**: two threads read, modify and write the same value;
  - **check-then-act**: a condition is checked, and another thread changes it before the action.
- They are hard to find: the code passes tests and fails under load.

## 3.2 · Lost update

`count++` is three steps: read, add, write. Two threads can read the same value, and one of the updates is lost.

```{.csharp}
class UnsafeCounter
{
    private int _count;

    public void Increment() => _count++;
    public void Decrement() => _count--;
    public int Count => _count;
}

var unsafeCounter = new UnsafeCounter();
var incrementer = new Thread(() =>
{
    for (var i = 0; i < 1_000_000; i++)
    {
        unsafeCounter.Increment();
    }
});
var decrementer = new Thread(() =>
{
    for (var i = 0; i < 1_000_000; i++)
    {
        unsafeCounter.Decrement();
    }
});

incrementer.Start();
decrementer.Start();
incrementer.Join();
decrementer.Join();

// 0 is expected, but almost every run prints something else
Console.WriteLine(unsafeCounter.Count);
```

## 3.3 · Check-then-act

- Checking a condition and acting on it are two separate steps; another thread can act in between.
- A thread-safe collection does not help: each call is safe, but the combination is not.
- The word game from lecture 7 has this pattern in `GameService.CompleteGame` (`Find`, then `Remove`): two simultaneous submissions both get experience.

## 3.4 · Check-then-act in code

```{.csharp}
var games = new ConcurrentDictionary<string, string>();
games["player@example.com"] = "game-1";
var awarded = 0;
var start = new Barrier(2);

void CompleteGame()
{
    start.SignalAndWait(); // both threads continue at the same moment

    // Check...
    if (games.ContainsKey("player@example.com"))
    {
        Thread.Sleep(10); // e.g. checking the answers
        // ...then act
        games.TryRemove("player@example.com", out _);
        Interlocked.Increment(ref awarded);
    }
}

var firstSubmission = new Thread(CompleteGame);
var secondSubmission = new Thread(CompleteGame);
firstSubmission.Start();
secondSubmission.Start();
firstSubmission.Join();
secondSubmission.Join();

Console.WriteLine($"Experience awarded {awarded} times");
```

## 3.5 · Making check-then-act atomic

`TryRemove` checks and removes in one atomic step, so only one thread can succeed.

```{.csharp}
games["player@example.com"] = "game-1";
awarded = 0;
start = new Barrier(2);

void CompleteGameAtomically()
{
    start.SignalAndWait();

    if (games.TryRemove("player@example.com", out _))
    {
        Interlocked.Increment(ref awarded);
    }
}

firstSubmission = new Thread(CompleteGameAtomically);
secondSubmission = new Thread(CompleteGameAtomically);
firstSubmission.Start();
secondSubmission.Start();
firstSubmission.Join();
secondSubmission.Join();

Console.WriteLine($"Experience awarded {awarded} times");
```

## 3.6 · Ways to avoid race conditions

| Approach | Tools |
|---|---|
| No shared mutable state | Immutable objects, data owned by a single thread |
| Atomic operations | `Interlocked`, single calls of concurrent collections (`TryRemove`, `GetOrAdd`) |
| Mutual exclusion | `lock`, `SemaphoreSlim` |
| Message passing | `Channel<T>` |

## 4.1 · `lock`

`lock` allows only one thread at a time into a block of code, a **critical section**. Since .NET 9 the lock object is of the `System.Threading.Lock` type.

```{.csharp}
class Counter
{
    private readonly Lock _lock = new();
    private int _count;

    public void Increment()
    {
        lock (_lock)
        {
            _count++;
        }
    }

    public void Decrement()
    {
        lock (_lock)
        {
            _count--;
        }
    }

    public int Count
    {
        get
        {
            lock (_lock)
            {
                return _count;
            }
        }
    }
}
```

## 4.2 · `lock` in use

```{.csharp}
var counter = new Counter();
var lockedIncrementer = new Thread(() =>
{
    for (var i = 0; i < 1_000_000; i++)
    {
        counter.Increment();
    }
});
var lockedDecrementer = new Thread(() =>
{
    for (var i = 0; i < 1_000_000; i++)
    {
        counter.Decrement();
    }
});

lockedIncrementer.Start();
lockedDecrementer.Start();
lockedIncrementer.Join();
lockedDecrementer.Join();

Console.WriteLine(counter.Count);
```

## 4.3 · Rules for `lock`

- The lock object only marks the critical section; it has no connection to the data. `_count` is protected only because every access to it is inside `lock (_lock)`.
- The lock object is `private readonly`. Never lock on `this`, a `Type` or a string: other code can lock on them too.
- Before .NET 9, any reference type was used: `private readonly object _lock = new();`.
- Critical sections are kept short. Unknown code (callbacks, events) is not called while holding a lock.
- `await` is not allowed inside `lock` (compile error CS1996). `SemaphoreSlim` is used instead.

## 4.4 · `Monitor` class

`lock` on an `object` is compiled to `Monitor` calls inside `try`/`finally`:

```csharp
lock (locker)
{
    Console.WriteLine("Entered");
}

// is compiled to approximately
var lockTaken = false;
try
{
    Monitor.Enter(locker, ref lockTaken);
    Console.WriteLine("Entered");
}
finally
{
    if (lockTaken)
    {
        Monitor.Exit(locker);
    }
}
```

- `finally` releases the lock even if an exception is thrown.
- `lock` on the `Lock` type is compiled to `Lock.EnterScope()` instead.

## 4.5 · `Monitor.TryEnter`

`Monitor` is used directly when waiting has to be limited: `Monitor.TryEnter(locker, timeout)` returns `false` instead of waiting forever. `Lock.TryEnter` does the same.

```{.csharp}
var resource = new object();

var holder = new Thread(() =>
{
    lock (resource)
    {
        Thread.Sleep(500);
    }
});
holder.Start();
Thread.Sleep(50); // lets the holder take the lock first

if (Monitor.TryEnter(resource, TimeSpan.FromMilliseconds(100)))
{
    try
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Lock acquired");
    }
    finally
    {
        Monitor.Exit(resource);
    }
}
else
{
    Console.WriteLine("Lock not acquired within 100 ms");
}

holder.Join();
```

## 4.6 · Signalling with `Monitor.Wait` and `Monitor.Pulse`

`Wait` and `Pulse` are not a deadlock tool. They are used when a thread waits for a condition that another thread makes true (a **condition variable**).

- `Monitor.Wait(locker)`: releases the lock and blocks until pulsed, then takes the lock again.
- `Monitor.Pulse(locker)`: wakes up one waiting thread; `PulseAll` wakes up all of them.
- Both are called while holding the lock.
- The condition is checked in a `while` loop: a pulse sent before `Wait` is lost, and a woken thread has to check again.

## 4.7 · `Wait` and `Pulse` in code

```{.csharp}
var gate = new object();
var items = new Queue<int>();

var consumerThread = new Thread(() =>
{
    for (var received = 0; received < 3; received++)
    {
        int item;
        lock (gate)
        {
            while (items.Count == 0)
            {
                Monitor.Wait(gate); // releases the lock while waiting
            }
            item = items.Dequeue();
        }
        Console.WriteLine($"Consumed {item}");
    }
});
consumerThread.Start();

for (var i = 1; i <= 3; i++)
{
    Thread.Sleep(100);
    lock (gate)
    {
        items.Enqueue(i);
        Console.WriteLine($"Produced {i}");
        Monitor.Pulse(gate);
    }
}

consumerThread.Join();
```

## 4.8 · `Interlocked`

`Interlocked` provides atomic operations on single variables: no other thread can see the operation half done.

- `Increment`, `Decrement`, `Add`: change an `int` or `long` and return the new value.
- `Exchange`: sets a new value and returns the old one.
- `CompareExchange`: sets a new value only if the current value equals the expected one, and returns the original value. Lock-free algorithms are built on it.
- `Read`: reads a 64-bit value atomically (needed on 32-bit platforms).

`Volatile.Read` and `Volatile.Write` make sure that a value written by one thread is seen by the others, without being cached or reordered.

## 4.9 · `Interlocked` in use

```{.csharp}
class InterlockedCounter
{
    private int _count;

    public void Increment() => Interlocked.Increment(ref _count);
    public void Decrement() => Interlocked.Decrement(ref _count);
    public int Count => Volatile.Read(ref _count);
}

var interlockedCounter = new InterlockedCounter();
var atomicIncrementer = new Thread(() =>
{
    for (var i = 0; i < 1_000_000; i++)
    {
        interlockedCounter.Increment();
    }
});
var atomicDecrementer = new Thread(() =>
{
    for (var i = 0; i < 1_000_000; i++)
    {
        interlockedCounter.Decrement();
    }
});

atomicIncrementer.Start();
atomicDecrementer.Start();
atomicIncrementer.Join();
atomicDecrementer.Join();

Console.WriteLine(interlockedCounter.Count);
```

## 4.10 · `CompareExchange`

```{.csharp}
var highScore = 0;

void ReportScore(int score)
{
    int current;
    do
    {
        current = Volatile.Read(ref highScore);
        if (score <= current)
        {
            return;
        }
    }
    // Retried if another thread changed highScore after it was read
    while (Interlocked.CompareExchange(ref highScore, score, current) != current);
}

Parallel.For(0, 1000, i => ReportScore(i % 997));
Console.WriteLine($"High score: {highScore}");
```

## 4.11 · Immutable data

- Data that never changes is safe to share between threads without any locks.
- A `record` with init-only properties is immutable; `with` creates a changed copy.
- `System.Collections.Immutable` provides `ImmutableList<T>`, `ImmutableDictionary<TKey, TValue>` and others.
- An update replaces the reference to the whole object, e.g. with `Interlocked.Exchange`.
- The word game `Game` is a record for this reason.

```{.csharp}
record GameState(string Player, int Score);

var state = new GameState("player@example.com", 0);

// Other threads can keep using the old object; it never changes
var updated = state with { Score = 30 };

Console.WriteLine(state);
Console.WriteLine(updated);
```

## 5.1 · Concurrent collections

Thread-safe collections in `System.Collections.Concurrent`:

- `ConcurrentDictionary<TKey, TValue>`: a dictionary.
- `ConcurrentQueue<T>`: first in, first out.
- `ConcurrentStack<T>`: last in, first out.
- `ConcurrentBag<T>`: an unordered collection, optimized for threads that both add and take items. It is not a replacement for `List<T>`: there is no order and no indexing.

Each single method call is atomic; a combination of calls is not (see check-then-act). Enumerating does not throw if the collection is changed at the same time.

## 5.2 · `ConcurrentDictionary`

- `TryAdd`: adds the pair only if the key is missing; returns `false` and changes nothing if it exists.
- `TryGetValue`, `TryRemove`: get or remove the value if the key exists.
- `TryUpdate(key, newValue, expected)`: updates only if the current value equals `expected`.
- `GetOrAdd`, `AddOrUpdate`: check and change in one call. The factory delegate can run more than once when threads race (only one result is stored), so it must not have side effects.
- The indexer `dict[key] = value` adds or overwrites.

`Try...` methods return `false` instead of throwing, because the state can change between a check and the call.

## 5.3 · `ConcurrentDictionary` in use

```{.csharp}
var fruits = new ConcurrentDictionary<int, string>();

fruits.TryAdd(1, "Apple");
fruits.TryAdd(2, "Banana");
Console.WriteLine($"Adding an existing key: {fruits.TryAdd(1, "Avocado")}, value stays {fruits[1]}");

// Updated only if the current value is still "Banana"
fruits.TryUpdate(2, "Blueberry", "Banana");

var cherry = fruits.GetOrAdd(3, key => "Cherry");
fruits.AddOrUpdate(1, "Apricot", (key, old) => old + " pie");

if (fruits.TryRemove(3, out var removedFruit))
{
    Console.WriteLine($"Removed key 3, which had value {removedFruit}");
}

foreach (var (key, fruit) in fruits.OrderBy(pair => pair.Key))
{
    Console.WriteLine($"{key}: {fruit}");
}
```

## 5.4 · Counting words in parallel

```{.csharp}
var words = "the cat and the dog and the bird".Split(' ');
var wordCounts = new ConcurrentDictionary<string, int>();

// Read, add one and write in a single atomic call
Parallel.ForEach(words, word => wordCounts.AddOrUpdate(word, 1, (_, count) => count + 1));

foreach (var (word, count) in wordCounts.OrderBy(pair => pair.Key))
{
    Console.WriteLine($"{word}: {count}");
}
```

## 5.5 · `ConcurrentQueue<T>` and `ConcurrentStack<T>`

- `Enqueue(T)` / `Push(T)`: adds an item.
- `TryDequeue(out T)` / `TryPop(out T)`: removes and returns an item, if there is one.
- `TryPeek(out T)`: returns the next item without removing it.

```{.csharp}
var queue = new ConcurrentQueue<string>();
queue.Enqueue("Apple");
queue.Enqueue("Banana");

if (queue.TryDequeue(out var dequeued))
{
    Console.WriteLine($"Dequeued: {dequeued}");
}

var stack = new ConcurrentStack<string>();
stack.Push("Apple");
stack.Push("Banana");

if (stack.TryPop(out var popped))
{
    Console.WriteLine($"Popped: {popped}");
}
```

## 5.6 · `ConcurrentBag<T>`

- `Add(T)`: adds an item.
- `TryTake(out T)`: removes and returns some item; which one is not defined.

```{.csharp}
var bag = new ConcurrentBag<string>();

Parallel.For(0, 5, i => bag.Add($"Item {i}"));

if (bag.TryTake(out var taken))
{
    Console.WriteLine($"Took: {taken}");
}

Console.WriteLine($"Items left: {bag.Count}");
```

## 6.1 · Deadlocks

A **deadlock** is a state where two or more threads each wait for a resource held by another, so none of them can continue. It happens only when all four conditions hold (Coffman, 1971):

1. **Mutual exclusion**: a resource is held by one thread at a time.
2. **Hold and wait**: a thread holds one resource while waiting for another.
3. **No preemption**: a resource cannot be taken away from a thread.
4. **Circular wait**: threads wait for each other in a cycle.

Breaking any one condition prevents deadlocks. Usually the circular wait is broken.

## 6.2 · Deadlock example

```{.csharp}
class BankAccount(int id, decimal balance)
{
    private readonly Lock _lock = new();

    public int Id { get; } = id;
    public decimal Balance { get; private set; } = balance;

    public void Transfer(BankAccount target, decimal amount)
    {
        lock (_lock)
        {
            Console.WriteLine($"{Thread.CurrentThread.Name}: locked account {Id}");
            Thread.Sleep(100); // gives the other thread time to lock its account

            Console.WriteLine($"{Thread.CurrentThread.Name}: waiting for account {target.Id}");
            lock (target._lock)
            {
                Balance -= amount;
                target.Balance += amount;
            }
        }
    }
}
```

## 6.3 · Running into the deadlock

```{.csharp}
var account1 = new BankAccount(1, 1000);
var account2 = new BankAccount(2, 1000);

// Opposite directions: each thread holds one lock and waits for the other.
// Background threads, so that the stuck threads do not keep the process alive.
var transfer1 = new Thread(() => account1.Transfer(account2, 100)) { Name = "Thread-1", IsBackground = true };
var transfer2 = new Thread(() => account2.Transfer(account1, 200)) { Name = "Thread-2", IsBackground = true };

transfer1.Start();
transfer2.Start();

// Join() would wait forever; with a timeout the deadlock is detected
var transfer1Done = transfer1.Join(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(1));
var transfer2Done = transfer2.Join(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(1));
Console.WriteLine(transfer1Done && transfer2Done ? "Completed" : "Deadlocked");
```

## 6.4 · Avoiding deadlocks with lock ordering

All threads take the locks in the same order, so a circular wait is impossible.

```{.csharp}
class OrderedBankAccount(int id, decimal balance)
{
    private readonly Lock _lock = new();
    public int Id { get; } = id;
    public decimal Balance { get; private set; } = balance;

    public void Transfer(OrderedBankAccount target, decimal amount)
    {
        // The account with the smaller id is always locked first
        var (first, second) = Id < target.Id ? (this, target) : (target, this);

        lock (first._lock)
        {
            Thread.Sleep(100);
            lock (second._lock)
            {
                Balance -= amount;
                target.Balance += amount;
            }
        }
    }
}
```

## 6.5 · Lock ordering in use

```{.csharp}
var ordered1 = new OrderedBankAccount(1, 1000);
var ordered2 = new OrderedBankAccount(2, 1000);

var orderedTransfer1 = new Thread(() => ordered1.Transfer(ordered2, 100));
var orderedTransfer2 = new Thread(() => ordered2.Transfer(ordered1, 200));
orderedTransfer1.Start();
orderedTransfer2.Start();
orderedTransfer1.Join();
orderedTransfer2.Join();

Console.WriteLine($"Account 1: {ordered1.Balance}, account 2: {ordered2.Balance}");
```

## 6.6 · Other ways to avoid deadlocks

- Hold only one lock at a time.
- Wait with a timeout (`TryEnter`), release everything and retry.
- Databases detect deadlocks between transactions themselves and abort one of them (see transactions in lecture 8).

## 7.1 · `Task`

- `Task` represents an operation that completes in the future (a promise). `Task<TResult>` also produces a value.
- A task is not a thread. A task waiting for I/O uses no thread at all; CPU work in a task runs on a thread pool thread.
- Tasks returned by `async` methods are already running ("hot").
- The result of a task is waited for with `await`.

## 7.2 · `async` and `await`

- `async` allows `await` inside the method and wraps the result in a task:
  - `void` becomes `Task`;
  - `TResult` becomes `Task<TResult>`.
- An `async` method runs **synchronously**, on the caller's thread, until the first `await` of an unfinished task. Only then does the caller get the task back and continue.
- When the awaited operation completes, the rest of the method (the **continuation**) is run. In console apps and ASP.NET Core it runs on a thread pool thread, possibly a different one.

```{.csharp}
async Task MethodAsync()
{
    Console.WriteLine($"Entered the method on thread {Environment.CurrentManagedThreadId}");
    await Task.Delay(100);
    Console.WriteLine($"Resumed on thread {Environment.CurrentManagedThreadId}");
}

Console.WriteLine($"Calling on thread {Environment.CurrentManagedThreadId}");
var methodTask = MethodAsync();
Console.WriteLine("Got the task back, the method is still waiting");
await methodTask;
Console.WriteLine("Method completed");
```

## 7.3 · How `await` works

The compiler rewrites an `async` method into a **state machine**:

- each `await` is a point where the method can pause;
- if the awaited task is already complete, execution simply continues;
- otherwise the local variables and the position are saved, a continuation is registered on the task, and the method returns;
- when the task completes, the continuation resumes the method from the saved position.

While an I/O operation (network, disk) is awaited, **no thread** waits for it: the operating system notifies .NET when it is done.

## 7.4 · `await` step by step

```{mermaid}
sequenceDiagram
    participant Caller
    participant Method as MethodAsync
    participant OS as Timer / I/O
    Caller->>Method: call (runs synchronously until await)
    Method->>OS: starts the operation
    Method-->>Caller: returns an unfinished Task
    Note over Caller: continues with other work
    Note over OS: no thread waits for the operation
    OS->>Method: completed: the rest of the method runs
    Method-->>Caller: Task completed
```

## 7.5 · How the completion gets back

- The operation is handed over together with the task that has to be completed:
  - `Task.Delay` registers a timer in the runtime's timer queue;
  - I/O is passed to the operating system (network card, disk driver).
- When it finishes, the operating system queues a completion notification: I/O completion ports on Windows, `epoll` on Linux, `kqueue` on macOS.
- A few runtime threads wait for these notifications for all operations at once and mark the matching task as completed.
- Completing a task queues its continuation to the thread pool (or to the UI thread, through the `SynchronizationContext`).
- A thread pool thread takes it from the queue and runs the rest of the method.

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    Device["Timer / network card / disk"] --> OS["OS completion queue"]
    OS --> Poller["Runtime I/O thread"]
    Poller --> Task["Task completed"]
    Task --> Queue["Thread pool queue"]
    Queue --> Rest["Rest of the method runs"]
```

## 7.6 · `async void`

- An `async void` method cannot be awaited: the caller cannot know when it has finished.
- It is used only for event handlers, whose signature is fixed. Everywhere else `Task` is returned.

```{.csharp}
async void SaveVoidAsync()
{
    await Task.Delay(100);
    Console.WriteLine("Saved");
}

SaveVoidAsync(); // there is no task to await
Console.WriteLine("Caller continues before saving has finished");

// The only way to wait is to guess how long it takes
Thread.Sleep(200);
```

```{.csharp}
async Task SaveAsync()
{
    await Task.Delay(100);
    Console.WriteLine("Saved");
}

await SaveAsync();
Console.WriteLine("Caller continues after saving");
```

## 7.7 · Exceptions in `async void`

An exception thrown in an `async void` method cannot be caught by the caller: there is no task to store it in, so it crashes the process.

```csharp
async void FailVoidAsync()
{
    await Task.Delay(10);
    throw new InvalidOperationException("Save failed");
}

try
{
    FailVoidAsync(); // returns at the first await
}
catch (InvalidOperationException)
{
    // Never reached: the exception is thrown later, on a thread pool thread,
    // and the whole process crashes
}
```

## 7.8 · Exceptions in `async Task`

- An exception thrown in an `async Task` method is stored in its task and thrown again when the task is awaited.
- A task that is never awaited hides its exception.

```{.csharp}
async Task FailAsync(string message)
{
    await Task.Delay(10);
    throw new InvalidOperationException(message);
}

try
{
    await FailAsync("Save failed");
}
catch (InvalidOperationException e)
{
    Console.WriteLine($"Caught: {e.Message}");
}
```

## 7.9 · Exceptions with `Task.WhenAll`

`await Task.WhenAll(...)` throws only the **first** exception; all of them are in `task.Exception` (an `AggregateException`).

```{.csharp}
var all = Task.WhenAll(FailAsync("first"), FailAsync("second"));

try
{
    await all;
}
catch (InvalidOperationException e)
{
    Console.WriteLine($"Caught: {e.Message}");
    Console.WriteLine($"All errors: {string.Join(", ", all.Exception!.InnerExceptions.Select(x => x.Message))}");
}
```

## 7.10 · Hidden `async void`

An `async` lambda passed as an `Action` is `async void` too, with the same problems:

```csharp
// Thread takes an Action: the thread ends at the first await,
// and an exception after it crashes the process
new Thread(async () => await SaveAsync()).Start();

// List<T>.ForEach takes an Action<T>: ForEach returns before any player is notified
players.ForEach(async player => await NotifyAsync(player));

// Fixed: the lambdas return tasks, which are awaited
await Task.WhenAll(players.Select(player => NotifyAsync(player)));
```

## 7.11 · Running operations at the same time

```{.csharp}
int SlowCalculation()
{
    // Keeps one core busy for 500 ms
    var busy = Stopwatch.StartNew();
    while (busy.ElapsedMilliseconds < 500)
    {
    }
    return 42;
}

async Task<string> CallApiAsync()
{
    await Task.Delay(500); // stands in for an HTTP call
    return "{ \"name\": \"Luke Skywalker\" }";
}

var sequentialStopwatch = Stopwatch.StartNew();
var apiResponse = await CallApiAsync();
var calculation = SlowCalculation();
Console.WriteLine($"One after another: {sequentialStopwatch.ElapsedMilliseconds} ms");
```

## 7.12 · Starting both before awaiting

```{.csharp}
var concurrentStopwatch = Stopwatch.StartNew();

// Both are started before either of them is awaited
var apiTask = CallApiAsync();
var calculationTask = Task.Run(SlowCalculation);

await Task.WhenAll(apiTask, calculationTask);
Console.WriteLine($"Calculation: {await calculationTask}, API: {await apiTask}");
Console.WriteLine($"At the same time: {concurrentStopwatch.ElapsedMilliseconds} ms");
```

- `Task.Run` is needed for the calculation: it has no `await`, so calling it directly would run it synchronously.
- Real HTTP calls use an `HttpClient` from `IHttpClientFactory`. A `new HttpClient()` per call exhausts the available sockets under load.

## 7.13 · Non-blocking delay

- `Thread.Sleep()` blocks the current thread.
- `await Task.Delay()` registers a timer and releases the thread; the method continues when the time has passed.

100 operations that each wait for 100 ms:

```{.csharp}
var sleepStopwatch = Stopwatch.StartNew();
// Each wait occupies a thread pool thread; the pool has to add threads one by one
await Task.WhenAll(Enumerable.Range(0, 100).Select(_ => Task.Run(() => Thread.Sleep(100))));
Console.WriteLine($"Thread.Sleep: {sleepStopwatch.ElapsedMilliseconds} ms, thread pool grew to {ThreadPool.ThreadCount} threads");

var delayStopwatch = Stopwatch.StartNew();
// No thread is occupied while waiting: all 100 timers run at the same time
await Task.WhenAll(Enumerable.Range(0, 100).Select(_ => Task.Delay(100)));
Console.WriteLine($"Task.Delay: {delayStopwatch.ElapsedMilliseconds} ms");
```

## 7.14 · Thread blocking example with `Task.Delay`

The same 10 actions as on slide 2.12 (Thread blocking), with `await Task.Delay` instead of `Thread.Sleep`:

```{.csharp}
var asyncStopwatch = Stopwatch.StartNew();
var startingThreads = new ConcurrentDictionary<int, bool>();

async Task RunActionAsync(int id)
{
    startingThreads.TryAdd(Environment.CurrentManagedThreadId, true);
    if (id % 2 == 0)
    {
        Console.WriteLine($"Action {id}: quick");
    }
    else
    {
        Console.WriteLine($"Action {id}: waiting...");
        await Task.Delay(500); // e.g. an async database call
    }
}

await Task.WhenAll(Enumerable.Range(0, 10).Select(id => RunActionAsync(id)));

Console.WriteLine($"Took {asyncStopwatch.ElapsedMilliseconds} ms, started by {startingThreads.Count} thread(s)");
```

## 7.15 · Starting a task

- A task returned by an `async` method is already running.
- `Task.Run` queues the work to the thread pool and returns a running task.
- `new Task(...)` creates an unstarted ("cold") task that needs `Start()`. It is almost never needed.

```{.csharp}
await Task.Run(() => Console.WriteLine($"Running on thread pool thread: {Thread.CurrentThread.IsThreadPoolThread}"));
```

```{.csharp}
var coldTask = new Task(() => Console.WriteLine("Cold task running"));
Console.WriteLine($"Status before Start: {coldTask.Status}");
coldTask.Start();
await coldTask;
```

## 7.16 · Where continuations run

- 100 tasks do not need 100 threads: the continuations are run by a few thread pool threads.
- In UI apps the continuation returns to the UI thread (through the `SynchronizationContext`), so controls can be updated after `await`.
- Console apps and ASP.NET Core have no `SynchronizationContext`; continuations run on any thread pool thread.

```{.csharp}
var usedThreads = new ConcurrentDictionary<int, bool>();

var manyTasks = Enumerable.Range(0, 100).Select(async _ =>
{
    for (var j = 0; j < 10; j++)
    {
        await Task.Delay(1);
        usedThreads.TryAdd(Environment.CurrentManagedThreadId, true);
    }
});

await Task.WhenAll(manyTasks);
Console.WriteLine($"100 tasks ran on {usedThreads.Count} threads");
```

## 7.17 · `ConfigureAwait(false)`

- `await task.ConfigureAwait(false)` tells that the continuation does not need to return to the original context (e.g. the UI thread).
- It is used in library code (NuGet packages), which may be called from UI apps.
- Application code in ASP.NET Core does not need it, as there is no `SynchronizationContext`.

## 8.1 · `Task.WhenAll` and `Task.WhenAny`

```{.csharp}
async Task<int> WaitAsync(int milliseconds)
{
    await Task.Delay(milliseconds);
    return milliseconds;
}

// Waits for all tasks; results are in the order of the tasks, not of completion
int[] results = await Task.WhenAll(WaitAsync(300), WaitAsync(100), WaitAsync(200));
Console.WriteLine($"All completed: {string.Join(", ", results)}");
```

```{.csharp}
var slowOperation = WaitAsync(1000);
var timeout = Task.Delay(200);

// Waits for the first task to complete
var winner = await Task.WhenAny(slowOperation, timeout);
Console.WriteLine(winner == timeout ? "Timed out" : "Completed in time");
```

## 8.2 · `Task.WhenEach`

Since .NET 9, `Task.WhenEach` returns the tasks in the order they complete, as an async stream that is read with `await foreach`:

```{.csharp}
var waits = new[] { WaitAsync(300), WaitAsync(100), WaitAsync(200) };

await foreach (var completedTask in Task.WhenEach(waits))
{
    Console.WriteLine($"Completed after {await completedTask} ms");
}
```

## 8.3 · `CancellationToken`

- A `CancellationToken` signals an operation that it should stop. It is created by a `CancellationTokenSource`.
- Most async APIs accept a token; it is passed down through every method.
- A cancelled operation throws `OperationCanceledException`, and its task ends in the `Canceled` state.
- CPU-bound loops call `cancellationToken.ThrowIfCancellationRequested()`.

## 8.4 · Cancelling work

```{.csharp}
async Task DoWorkAsync(CancellationToken cancellationToken)
{
    for (var i = 0; i < 10; i++)
    {
        Console.WriteLine($"Working on item {i}");
        // The token is passed on, so the delay itself is cancelled
        await Task.Delay(100, cancellationToken);
    }
    Console.WriteLine("Work completed");
}

using (var source = new CancellationTokenSource())
{
    source.CancelAfter(TimeSpan.FromMilliseconds(350));
    var work = DoWorkAsync(source.Token);
    try
    {
        await work;
    }
    catch (OperationCanceledException)
    {
        Console.WriteLine($"Work cancelled, task status: {work.Status}");
    }
}
```

## 8.5 · Cancellation in ASP.NET Core

An endpoint parameter of type `CancellationToken` is cancelled when the client disconnects (`HttpContext.RequestAborted`):

```csharp
app.MapGet("/leaderboard", async (WordGameContext db, CancellationToken cancellationToken) =>
    await db.Users
        .OrderByDescending(u => u.Experience)
        .Take(10)
        .ToListAsync(cancellationToken));
```

## 8.6 · Tasks without asynchrony

When a method has to return a `Task` (e.g. because of an interface), but has nothing to wait for, a completed task is created:

- `Task.FromResult(value)` wraps a value into a completed `Task<T>`.
- `Task.CompletedTask` is a completed `Task` without a value.

```{.csharp}
Task<bool> TaskWithResultAsync()
{
    return Task.FromResult(true);
}

Task TaskWithoutResultAsync()
{
    return Task.CompletedTask;
}

var taskResult = await TaskWithResultAsync();
Console.WriteLine($"Completed with result {taskResult}");

await TaskWithoutResultAsync();
Console.WriteLine("Completed without result");
```

## 8.7 · `ValueTask`

- `ValueTask<T>` is an alternative for methods that usually complete synchronously, e.g. returning a cached value.
- It avoids allocating a `Task`.
- A `ValueTask` may be awaited only once.
- `Task` is the default choice.

## 8.8 · Blocking on async code

- `.Result`, `.Wait()` and `.GetAwaiter().GetResult()` block the current thread until a task completes ("sync over async").
- It is avoided: once a method is `async`, its callers become `async` too ("async all the way").
- In UI apps (and the old ASP.NET) it causes a **deadlock**: the UI thread waits for the task, and the task's continuation waits for the UI thread.
- In ASP.NET Core there is no deadlock, but each waiting request holds a thread pool thread, which leads to thread pool starvation under load.
- `.Result` and `.Wait()` wrap exceptions in `AggregateException`; `.GetAwaiter().GetResult()` does not.

```{.csharp}
async Task<int> DelayAndReturnAsync(int value)
{
    await Task.Delay(100);
    return value;
}

// Works in a console app, but the thread is blocked for 100 ms
var blockedResult = DelayAndReturnAsync(42).GetAwaiter().GetResult();
Console.WriteLine($"Result: {blockedResult}");
```

## 8.9 · Deadlock in a UI app

```csharp
// WinForms: this click handler never completes
private void Button_Click(object sender, EventArgs e)
{
    // The UI thread blocks here, waiting for the task...
    var value = DelayAndReturnAsync(42).Result;
    resultLabel.Text = value.ToString();
}
// ...while the continuation after `await Task.Delay` waits for the UI thread.

// Fixed: the event handler is async (async void is allowed for event handlers)
private async void Button_Click(object sender, EventArgs e)
{
    var value = await DelayAndReturnAsync(42);
    resultLabel.Text = value.ToString();
}
```

## 9.1 · `SemaphoreSlim`

- `SemaphoreSlim` limits how many operations can be inside a section at the same time.
- `WaitAsync()` waits without blocking a thread, so it works in `async` code.
- It is released in `finally`, so that an exception does not leave it taken.

```{.csharp}
var semaphore = new SemaphoreSlim(2); // at most 2 at a time

async Task AccessLimitedResourceAsync(int id)
{
    await semaphore.WaitAsync();
    try
    {
        Console.WriteLine($"Task {id} entered");
        await Task.Delay(200);
        Console.WriteLine($"Task {id} leaving");
    }
    finally
    {
        semaphore.Release();
    }
}

var semaphoreStopwatch = Stopwatch.StartNew();
await Task.WhenAll(Enumerable.Range(1, 5).Select(id => AccessLimitedResourceAsync(id)));
Console.WriteLine($"5 tasks of 200 ms, 2 at a time: {semaphoreStopwatch.ElapsedMilliseconds} ms");
```

## 9.2 · `SemaphoreSlim` as an async lock

`await` cannot be used inside `lock`. `SemaphoreSlim(1, 1)` lets only one operation in at a time and allows `await` inside:

```{.csharp}
class ScoreBoard
{
    private readonly SemaphoreSlim _mutex = new(1, 1);
    private int _total;

    public async Task AddAsync(int points)
    {
        await _mutex.WaitAsync();
        try
        {
            var current = _total;
            await Task.Delay(1); // e.g. saving to a database
            _total = current + points;
        }
        finally
        {
            _mutex.Release();
        }
    }

    public int Total => _total;
}

var board = new ScoreBoard();
await Task.WhenAll(Enumerable.Range(0, 20).Select(_ => board.AddAsync(10)));
Console.WriteLine($"Total: {board.Total}");
```

## 9.3 · Async streams

- `IAsyncEnumerable<T>` is a sequence whose items arrive asynchronously, one at a time.
- It is produced with `yield return` in an `async` method and read with `await foreach`.
- EF Core queries can be read this way (`AsAsyncEnumerable()`), and ASP.NET Core can stream them in a response.

```{.csharp}
async IAsyncEnumerable<int> ReadScoresAsync()
{
    for (var page = 1; page <= 3; page++)
    {
        await Task.Delay(100); // e.g. the next page from a database
        yield return page * 10;
    }
}

await foreach (var score in ReadScoresAsync())
{
    Console.WriteLine($"Score: {score}");
}
```

## 9.4 · Channels

`System.Threading.Channels` is an asynchronous producer/consumer queue:

- the writer and the reader both `await`: no polling and no blocked threads;
- a bounded channel makes the writer wait while it is full (**back-pressure**);
- a typical use is events from many requests processed by one background worker.

## 9.5 · Channels in use

```{.csharp}
using System.Threading.Channels;

var channel = Channel.CreateBounded<string>(capacity: 2);

var producer = Task.Run(async () =>
{
    for (var i = 1; i <= 5; i++)
    {
        await channel.Writer.WriteAsync($"guess {i}"); // waits while the channel is full
        Console.WriteLine($"Produced guess {i}");
    }
    channel.Writer.Complete();
});

var consumer = Task.Run(async () =>
{
    // Ends when the writer is completed and all items are read
    await foreach (var guess in channel.Reader.ReadAllAsync())
    {
        await Task.Delay(100); // slow processing
        Console.WriteLine($"Processed {guess}");
    }
});

await Task.WhenAll(producer, consumer);
```

## 9.6 · Background work in ASP.NET Core

- A `BackgroundService` runs long-running work: it is started with the application and stopped through `stoppingToken` on shutdown.
- `PeriodicTimer` is awaited for each tick, so runs never overlap.
- It is registered with `builder.Services.AddHostedService<ExpiredGameCleaner>()`.
- Hosted services are singletons: a scoped service such as a `DbContext` is taken from a new scope created with `IServiceScopeFactory`.
- An unhandled exception in `ExecuteAsync` stops the whole application, so errors inside the loop are caught and logged.
- In a real-time app, a background service can push updates to clients through SignalR (`IHubContext`).

## 9.7 · `BackgroundService` example

```csharp
public class ExpiredGameCleaner(IGameStore games, TimeProvider time, ILogger<ExpiredGameCleaner> logger)
    : BackgroundService
{
    protected override async Task ExecuteAsync(CancellationToken stoppingToken)
    {
        using var timer = new PeriodicTimer(TimeSpan.FromMinutes(1), time);

        while (await timer.WaitForNextTickAsync(stoppingToken))
        {
            // RemoveStartedBefore would be a new method of the lecture 7 game store
            var removed = games.RemoveStartedBefore(time.GetUtcNow() - GameService.TimeLimit);
            logger.LogInformation("Removed {Count} expired games", removed);
        }
    }
}
```

## 9.8 · `PeriodicTimer`

```{.csharp}
var timer = new PeriodicTimer(TimeSpan.FromMilliseconds(100));
var ticks = 0;

while (ticks < 3 && await timer.WaitForNextTickAsync())
{
    ticks++;
    Console.WriteLine($"Tick {ticks}");
}

timer.Dispose();
```

## 10.1 · Task parallel library

- `Parallel.For` and `Parallel.ForEach` split work across thread pool threads and block the caller until all of it is done.
- They speed up only CPU-bound work with enough work per item; for small items the overhead is bigger than the gain.
- The body runs on several threads at once, so shared state needs `Interlocked`, a lock or a concurrent collection.
- **Amdahl's law**: the sequential part limits the speed-up. If 90% of the work is parallel, 8 cores give at most $1 / (0.1 + 0.9 / 8) \approx 4.7$ times.
- One `Stopwatch` run is not a measurement; BenchmarkDotNet is used for that (lecture 15).

## 10.2 · Counting primes sequentially

```{.csharp}
bool IsPrime(int n)
{
    if (n < 2)
    {
        return false;
    }

    for (var divisor = 2; divisor * divisor <= n; divisor++)
    {
        if (n % divisor == 0)
        {
            return false;
        }
    }
    return true;
}

const int Limit = 3_000_000;

var sequentialPrimesStopwatch = Stopwatch.StartNew();
var sequentialCount = 0;
for (var i = 0; i < Limit; i++)
{
    if (IsPrime(i))
    {
        sequentialCount++;
    }
}
Console.WriteLine($"Sequential: {sequentialCount} primes in {sequentialPrimesStopwatch.ElapsedMilliseconds} ms");
```

## 10.3 · Counting primes with `Parallel.For`

```{.csharp}
var parallelStopwatch = Stopwatch.StartNew();
var parallelCount = 0;

Parallel.For(0, Limit, i =>
{
    if (IsPrime(i))
    {
        // parallelCount++ here would lose updates
        Interlocked.Increment(ref parallelCount);
    }
});

Console.WriteLine($"Parallel: {parallelCount} primes in {parallelStopwatch.ElapsedMilliseconds} ms");
```

## 10.4 · `Parallel.ForEachAsync`

For many I/O operations with a limit on how many run at the same time:

```{.csharp}
var fetchStopwatch = Stopwatch.StartNew();

await Parallel.ForEachAsync(
    Enumerable.Range(1, 10),
    new ParallelOptions { MaxDegreeOfParallelism = 3 },
    async (id, cancellationToken) =>
    {
        await Task.Delay(100, cancellationToken); // e.g. an HTTP call for one id
        Console.WriteLine($"Fetched {id}");
    });

Console.WriteLine($"10 calls, 3 at a time: {fetchStopwatch.ElapsedMilliseconds} ms");
```

## 10.5 · PLINQ

- PLINQ (Parallel LINQ) executes LINQ queries in parallel: `.AsParallel()`.
- The same rules apply: CPU-heavy work, lambdas without side effects.
- Results are unordered by default; `.AsOrdered()` keeps the source order at some cost.
- `.WithDegreeOfParallelism(n)` limits the number of threads.

```{.csharp}
var plinqStopwatch = Stopwatch.StartNew();
var plinqCount = Enumerable.Range(0, Limit).AsParallel().Count(IsPrime);
Console.WriteLine($"PLINQ: {plinqCount} primes in {plinqStopwatch.ElapsedMilliseconds} ms");

var firstPrimes = Enumerable.Range(0, 50).AsParallel().AsOrdered().Where(IsPrime).Take(5);
Console.WriteLine($"First primes: {string.Join(", ", firstPrimes)}");
```
